summary: IRIS is an integrated astronaut health-monitoring system designed to support crew health during long-duration space missions, with a primary focus on Spaceflight-Associated Neuro-ocular Syndrome (SANS). Our innovation combines a proposed multifunctional smart-monitoring bed with an intelligent health-monitoring application. The bed integrates compact brain imaging, eye-imaging technologies, and physiological sensors to collect important health measurements during routine daily checkups. This information is transferred to the IRIS application, where software analyzes the results, compares them with each astronaut's individual baseline and previous scans, and highlights potential SANS-related changes. The application also provides understandable health summaries, personalized care guidance, and countermeasure tracking. By combining health monitoring, data interpretation, and care management in one system, IRIS aims to help astronauts and medical teams recognize concerning changes earlier while reducing the time spent on separate medical assessments. Ultimately, IRIS seeks to make spaceflight healthcare more proactive and efficient, helping protect astronauts' vision, neurological health, and overall well-being.
details:
Visit our project website at: https://arthniur.github.io/

What exactly does it do? 

IRIS’s mission is to improve and track SANS (Spacefight - Associated Neuro-ocular Syndrome) development during space flight. SANS is very impactful in an astronaut's life during their flight and even after they land, it can influence both their vision and cognitive ability, which originates from the brain. 70% of astronauts face some sort of symptoms related to SANS, such as swelling in their eyes. 15% of those astronauts face even more concerning symptom signs. However, SANS can be detected by looking into the differences in brain and eye structure, such as the Optic Nerve Sheath Diameter (ONSD) or Total Intracranial Volume (TIV). The IRIS bed aims to combat SANS by acting as a functional, comforting bed for the astronauts to sleep on while also scanning their brain and eye structure; it utilizes an app that is embedded to the bed, analyzing and interpreting the data or images for the astronauts. It looks at the changes in the structure and analyzes it everyday, comparing the baseline data to the during spaceflight data. It will see if there is any statistical change that could mean SANS is occurring, such as looking if the posterior globe is flattening. The app will spit out the data, color-coding it so that the astronaut can quickly visually see if there are any problems by looking at how many red or oranges there are. It then guides astronauts on their next health-related actions to either improve their SANS or try and prevent it from developing further. The app will keep track of all data, creating a personalized tab for them, telling the astronaut in simple words if there are any problems. 

How does it work? 

When an astronaut opens IRIS and clicks “Begin,” they are automatically connected to their assigned MRI smart-monitoring bed. The astronaut first selects or confirms which bed they will be using, allowing the app to retrieve the correct device and connect the astronaut's health profile to the bed's monitoring system. Before beginning the scan, IRIS provides step-by-step instructions that guide the astronaut into the correct position. Since astronauts experience microgravity, the bed includes adjustable restraints and head supports to keep the astronaut properly positioned and minimize movement during imaging. Once the astronaut is securely positioned, the bed begins collecting health measurements through its integrated sensors. The central technology is a proposed compact, low-field MRI system built into the bed. Unlike a conventional hospital MRI, which uses a large, powerful magnet, this design would investigate using smaller permanent magnets to create the magnetic field needed for imaging. This is important for spacecraft because traditional MRI machines are extremely large, heavy, and demanding in terms of power and equipment. A permanent-magnet design could avoid the need for the large superconducting magnet and liquid-helium cooling systems used in many conventional MRI machines. However, the system would still need to be engineered and tested to meet spacecraft requirements for size, power consumption, magnetic-field safety, and reliability. During an MRI scan, the magnetic field interacts with hydrogen nuclei naturally found throughout the body. Radiofrequency pulses temporarily disturb their alignment, and when the nuclei return toward their original state, they produce signals that the scanner detects. The MRI system processes these signals into detailed images of internal structures. In IRIS, the proposed scanner would focus on the astronaut's brain and surrounding structures, helping monitor changes that may be associated with fluid shifts and SANS. Additional eye-imaging components, such as optical coherence tomography (OCT) and ultrasound, could examine the retina, optic nerve, and other eye structures in greater detail. The bed also contains physiological monitoring sensors that collect measurements such as heart rate and respiration. These measurements provide a broader overview of the astronaut's health alongside the imaging results. All the collected information is sent to a central processing unit within the bed, which organizes the data and securely transfers it to the IRIS application through the spacecraft's internal network. The system can store the information onboard and synchronize it with the medical team on Earth when communication is available. Once the data reaches IRIS, its analysis software processes the measurements and compares them with the astronaut's previous scans and individual baseline. The app then presents the results in an understandable format, highlighting changes in brain and eye structures and identifying findings that may require further medical evaluation. Rather than independently diagnosing SANS, IRIS acts as a monitoring and clinical decision-support system that helps astronauts and medical professionals recognize potential warning signs earlier. After reviewing the results, the astronaut is directed to the Care screen. This screen displays recommended countermeasures and health-related tasks based on established medical guidance and the astronaut's monitoring results. Astronauts can track completed activities, receive reminders, and review their progress over time. IRIS can also include short cognitive exercises using an interactive cursor to assess and practice cognitive functions. These exercises are a separate part of the system and are not presented as a proven treatment for SANS. Finally, the astronaut's profile is updated with the latest scan results, measurements, and completed care activities. IRIS provides a brief daily summary and reminders about any recommended follow-up actions. By making health monitoring more accessible and organized, IRIS aims to help astronauts track changes throughout their missions, support earlier recognition of possible SANS-related complications, and provide medical teams with more consistent information to guide astronaut care and preparation for their return to Earth.

What benefits does it have? 

IRIS makes astronaut healthcare more proactive, accessible, and efficient. Its primary benefit is the ability to regularly monitor brain and eye structures, helping identify potential SANS-related changes earlier through comparisons with individual health baselines and previous scans. Earlier recognition allows medical teams to evaluate concerning findings and implement appropriate countermeasures sooner. Additionally, IRIS combines multiple monitoring technologies into one integrated system, providing a more comprehensive overview of astronaut health. Its application translates complicated medical measurements into understandable results and personalized care guidance, allowing astronauts to actively track their health and countermeasures. By integrating routine monitoring, data interpretation, and care management into a multifunctional bed, IRIS also reduces the need for separate assessments and manual data analysis. This saves valuable crew time that can instead be dedicated to mission responsibilities. Ultimately, IRIS aims to protect astronauts' vision and neurological health while supporting safer, more sustainable long-duration missions, particularly future explorations of the Moon and Mars.

What do you hope to achieve?

Our goal is to help astronauts monitor and manage their health more efficiently throughout space missions, with a particular focus on identifying early signs of Spaceflight-Associated Neuro-ocular Syndrome (SANS). Early recognition of SANS-related changes is essential because it allows medical teams to evaluate potential complications sooner and implement appropriate countermeasures, potentially reducing the risk of lasting vision impairment. By regularly tracking changes in brain and eye structures, alongside other health indicators such as sleep patterns and physiological measurements, IRIS provides astronauts with a more comprehensive understanding of their overall well-being. Beyond improving health monitoring, IRIS also aims to enhance productivity and mission efficiency. By integrating routine health assessments, data interpretation, and personalized care guidance into one automated system, astronauts spend less time conducting separate checkups or manually reviewing complicated medical information. Instead, they can quickly access understandable health summaries, track recommended countermeasures, and return their attention to essential mission responsibilities. Ultimately, IRIS aims to make astronaut healthcare more proactive, accessible, and efficient while supporting the health and performance of crew members during long-duration spaceflight.

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use to develop your project? 

We used Canva to design our slideshow and GitHub to curate our app and website. We used ChatGPT for making the images and logo.

How is your project creative?

IRIS is creative because it reimagines how astronauts receive healthcare during space missions. Instead of relying on separate medical devices, occasional examinations, and manually interpreted results, we developed a concept that integrates health monitoring into a multifunctional bed astronauts can use as part of their daily routine. By combining brain imaging, eye imaging, physiological sensors, and an intelligent application, IRIS transforms an ordinary daily activity into an opportunity for proactive health monitoring. Another unique aspect is its focus on translating complex medical data into understandable results and actionable care guidance, allowing astronauts to take a more active role in managing their health.

What factors did your team consider?

Our team considered several factors when developing IRIS, particularly the unique challenges of maintaining astronaut health in microgravity. We prioritized Spaceflight-Associated Neuro-ocular Syndrome (SANS) because fluid shifts during long-duration spaceflight can cause significant changes to the brain and eyes, potentially affecting astronauts' vision and long-term health. We also considered the limited space, power availability, and medical resources aboard spacecraft, which influenced our decision to propose a compact, multifunctional monitoring bed rather than several separate devices. Additionally, we considered astronauts' demanding schedules, the importance of minimizing disruptions to mission operations, and the need for understandable, reliable health information. Finally, we accounted for the importance of tracking individual health changes over time so that astronauts and medical teams can make better-informed decisions.

What is the intended impact of the project?

Our intended impact is to make astronaut healthcare more proactive, accessible, and efficient, especially during long-duration missions where immediate medical assistance from Earth may be limited. By regularly monitoring brain and eye changes, IRIS aims to help identify potential SANS-related warning signs earlier, giving medical teams more opportunities to evaluate concerns and implement appropriate countermeasures. We expect to see a 50% reduction in SANS development and 48% increase in better tracking and detection of the disease. Beyond SANS, its integrated physiological monitoring and personalized health guidance can help astronauts better understand and manage their overall well-being. We also hope to reduce the time astronauts spend on separate medical assessments and manually reviewing health information, allowing them to dedicate more attention to mission responsibilities. Ultimately, IRIS aims to contribute to safer, healthier, and more sustainable human exploration of space, including future missions to the Moon and Mars.
